rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The only protection from Satan’s deceptive assaults is refuge with God; without constant vigilance, a person may be misled and find it hard to recover.
rows.anchor: the only way is to seek refuge with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next sūrah teaches God’s human-relevant attributes as the divinely disclosed means of refuge; only God knows which attributes shield people from Satan, and self-judgment risks error.
rows.anchor: the attributes of God by means of which he can attain refuge with God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next sūrah also exposes Satan’s reach, attack routes, and methods, helping people neither fear him excessively nor become heedless, and showing the defenses God gave them.
rows.anchor: the most effective of his

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although al-falaq is commonly rendered ‘morning,’ its underlying sense is splitting or tearing apart; morning is one example of something appearing when something else splits.
rows.anchor: its real meaning is “to tear apart something.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because many things emerge through splitting and the Qur’an uses the term broadly, he reads al-falaq in its wider contextual sense rather than restricting it to morning.
rows.anchor: In this writer’s opinion, keeping in view its placement and context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He translates rabb al-falaq as ‘He who brings forth,’ judging this fuller rendering more meaningful and suited to the subject that follows.
rows.anchor: as “He who brings forth.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should seek protection from created harms through their Creator alone: no other being can surpass the Creator’s power, so turning elsewhere is irrational.
rows.anchor: no one other than Him should be called upon for this purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God creates things for good purposes but may turn them into harm; rain can become punishment, and human ignorance or misuse can make a benefit harmful.
rows.anchor: Whatever God has created has been created for a positive purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One must not treat an object or person as independently powerful or invoke saints as ghawth or quṭub; ordinary means such as doctors are permissible when God alone is regarded as the true healer.
rows.anchor: seek refuge with God alone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse shuts out polytheism and dualism: calamities are created manifestations that act by God’s leave, and only God’s help can shield a person from them.
rows.anchor: to close many doors which lead to polytheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāsiq denotes night after dusk, and waqaba means darkness spreading; the phrase ‘when it spreads’ indicates night rather than the moon, despite a lexical view that ghāsiq can mean moon.
rows.anchor: clearly points to the fact that it means “the night.”

rows.speaker: lexicographers
rows.claim: Lexicographers also give ghāsiq the meaning ‘moon,’ a reading Islahi rejects here because the following phrase describes spreading darkness.
rows.anchor: Lexicographers have written that gh āsiq

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evil is not an independent creation requiring a separate creator; it is a by-product of created things, so refuge is sought from God alone.
rows.anchor: This verse is a very good example of the fact

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night sustains life through its calm, yet also shelters thieves, killers, enemies, and harmful creatures; both its benefit and harm come under one Creator, whose refuge is needed in every circumstance.
rows.anchor: the night which provides comfort to man has an evil by-product

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an elsewhere presents the day-night balance as evidence of monotheism; misunderstanding evil’s dependent nature leads some people to posit separate creators and dualism.
rows.anchor: for the sustenance of this world, just as the warmth of the day is necessary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage moves from material calamities to spiritual and moral evil.
rows.anchor: he is urged to seek refuge from evil which is spiritual and moral in nature.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-naffāthāt means those who blow on knots; its feminine form does not limit the agents to women, since Arabic usage permits evil spirits or souls, male or female.
rows.anchor: it can imply evil spirits and evil souls, whether men or women

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The possible agents include evil forces among Jews and Sabeans or Arabia’s conjurers and soothsayers.
rows.anchor: whether here they refer to those among the Jews and Sabeans or among the conjurers and soothsayers of Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Charmers chant spells while blowing on knotted cords or threads, pretending to control and harm their targets; the adjective paints this performance as worthless, like the soothsayers in 26:223.
rows.anchor: Blowing on knots is the way adopted by charmers and people who give amulets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most spells are fraud; any real harm they cause occurs only by God’s permission, so people need seek refuge with no one else.
rows.anchor: they can only cause any harm by God’s permission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God deals with people according to their own orientation: remembrance, trust, and turning to Him in hardship keep Satan from prevailing, and turning attention back to God helps when harm occurs.
rows.anchor: remains replete with His remembrance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A superstitious, credulous person who prefers conjecture and doubt to reason and trust becomes vulnerable to evil promptings from jinn and human devils.
rows.anchor: if a person is superstitious and credulous

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The remedy when the heart inclines toward evil is immediate refuge with God, best sought by reciting the Qur’an’s final two sūrahs.
rows.anchor: he should immediately seek refuge with Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The envious are addressed generally, not as one particular person; envy that crosses its limits, like Cain’s envy of Abel, may end in murder, so refuge should always be sought.
rows.anchor: no one specific is implied.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan is humanity’s greatest envier, especially of monotheistic faith; the cited threat illustrates the fierce determination behind ‘when he envies.’
rows.anchor: it is Satan who envies man the most and is particularly envious of the belief of monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording ‘when he envies’ depicts Satan unleashing his full frenzy, resources, and determination to divert humanity from monotheism.
rows.anchor: when this envious being starts to show his envy with full frenzy.

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some report that a Jewish magic spell made the Prophet ill and that he received this sūrah and recovered after reciting it.
rows.anchor: some people have mentioned it with reference to an incident as per which the Prophet (sws), God forbid, once came under

rows.speaker: some proponents of the narrative
rows.claim: They claim the spell did not impede prophetic duties, while also describing prolonged confusion in ordinary tasks, relations with his wives, and sight; Islahi asks how prayer or revelation could then be ruled out as affected.
rows.anchor: Although it is claimed that this magic spell did not in any way affect him in discharging his duties as a prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the spell as the sūrah’s occasion of revelation because it conflicts with the Qur’anic doctrine that prophets are protected when receiving and conveying revelation.
rows.anchor: it is against the established belief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Physical wounds or death do not undermine prophetic infallibility; a mental lapse caused by magic could compromise the prophet’s duties, so God’s protection is essential to preserve revealed religion.
rows.anchor: None of these happenings can hinder them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an attests that the Prophet received and communicated revelation reliably, and Muslims must affirm this.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) received and communicated

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi argues that the spell report has weak, solitary transmission: only Bukhārī, Muslim, and Ibn Mājah record it, it remained a khabar-i wāḥid through its third narrator, and Sufyān ibn ʿUyaynah said he first heard it from Ibn Jurayj; because a six-month event appeared in public accounts late, he argues it should have been famous early and mutawātir.
rows.anchor: weakness in the chain of narrators can be noted.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The collections do not specify a six-month duration; their shared wording indicates that any effect lasted only hours until the Prophet prayed through a day or night.
rows.anchor: it only lasted for some hours.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the event happened, Islahi compares it to Moses’ temporary alarm at the magicians’ ropes; such incidents may test prophets but remain transient and do not impair infallibility.
rows.anchor: can even take place to test the prophets

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical compilers did not link this incident to these sūrahs as an occasion of revelation or say the Prophet untied knots while reciting them; later scholars made that link, although the sūrahs’ themes reject it.
rows.anchor: the later scholars who have linked the narratives

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sūrah al-Nās is al-Falaq’s counterpart: both seek God’s protection from evils, with no essential difference in their central themes.
rows.anchor: there is no essential difference between the central themes of the two.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nās seeks refuge through attributes directly related to people, giving it a stronger appeal; al-Falaq is also compelling but argues more explicitly, while al-Nās’ repeated calls of mercy dominate.
rows.anchor: refuge is sought with God through His attributes which are directly related to human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where al-Falaq seeks refuge from varied evils, al-Nās targets Satan, the root of evil and the enduring enemy of monotheism.
rows.anchor: this sūrah seeks protection against Satan, the root of all evils

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Falaq foregrounds Satan’s envy, whereas al-Nās lays out his methods, accomplices, and avenues of attack so people can recognize and resist him.
rows.anchor: his method and technique, his clan and accomplices, the sphere of his incursions and onslaughts

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening attributes identify God’s basic rights over people and show that help should be sought only from one who possesses them.
rows.anchor: They guide us moreover that help should only be solicited from someone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The true Cherisher is rightly mankind’s Emperor, and the true Emperor alone has the right to worship; worshipping one who is neither is irrational and forbidden.
rows.anchor: who is the real Emperor of mankind to have the right

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This repeats al-Fātiḥah’s implication: because God cherishes creation, all gratitude belongs to Him, and He alone should be worshipped and asked for help.
rows.anchor: since it is the Almighty Who is the Cherisher of His creation, all thanksgiving must return to Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accepting the three attributes closes the doors to polytheism, and acknowledging any one entails acknowledging the others.
rows.anchor: closes all doors which lead to polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although unstated by name, Satan is the entity from whom refuge is sought, as the attributes and later specification make clear.
rows.anchor: it is quite evident from the attributes mentioned and the specification made later that it is Satan who is referred to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s technique is deceptive propaganda, promises, and wicked suggestions; after entrapping people, he leaves them to the consequences and watches their ruin.
rows.anchor: He allures people through propaganda and deceptive promises and by initiating wicked suggestions in their minds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waswās and khannās occur without a conjunction, indicating that both traits coexist in the prompter.
rows.anchor: There is no conjunction between

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s only weapon is prompting; he can frighten or cajole but cannot force astray or harm those who do not succumb, as God assures in 17:65.
rows.anchor: Apart from this, he has no other powers

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators generally define khannās as one who prompts while hidden, a reading that works only if Satan and his allies are considered jinn alone, whereas the final verse includes human devils too.
rows.anchor: Commentators have generally regarded it to mean someone who prompts evil suggestions while remaining hidden from people.

rows.speaker: some other commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators take khannās to mean one who comes again and again, but Islahi says this has no basis in Arabic.
rows.anchor: Some other commentators have understood it to mean “someone who comes again and again.” This has no basis in the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khannās means one who withdraws and retreats: Satan first entices, then disowns the consequences when his victim follows evil suggestions.
rows.anchor: someone who withdraws and retreats.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an illustrates Satan’s abandonment of followers by calling him a deceiver at 25:29.
rows.anchor: And Satan is the deceiver of men.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s promises are deceptive, as the cited verse 17:64 states.
rows.anchor: All of Satan’s promises are mere deception.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At 59:16, Satan induces disbelief and then disowns the person who follows him.
rows.anchor: I here and now disown you, I fear God, the Lord of the Worlds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Badr, the Jews displayed this satanic pattern by urging Quraysh to fight with assurances of support, then failing to appear, as shown in 8:48.
rows.anchor: The Jews had demonstrated this satanic character at the time of the battle of Badr.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evil leaders and followers will repeat Satan’s pattern in Hell: leaders will blame followers for choosing them and refuse responsibility for their punishment.
rows.anchor: that it was their fault that

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word khannās warns people not to be taken in by Satan’s sweet talk but to remember his betrayal when they fall for his promises.
rows.anchor: should not be overwhelmed by his sweet talk

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final verses explain Satan’s mission: he prompts evil in the bosom; ‘chests’ means the heart, and the suggestions aim to divert people from the right path without coercive power.
rows.anchor: actually implies a person’s heart

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘From among jinn and people’ identifies Satan’s brethren: any human or jinn who induces evil suggestions in others is a Satan, not a separate or eternal creation.
rows.anchor: is, in fact, a Satan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Satan who misled Adam was a jinn; the satanic mission continues until Judgment through followers among both jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: was from among the jinn.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In his closing prayer, Islahi asks God to show truth and falsehood clearly, enable people to follow the truth and avoid falsehood, and grants all gratitude to God.
rows.anchor: Show us the right path the way it is and make us follow it
